title: Compliance
summary: Every compliance guideline, why it exists, and the lies and promises that are automatic fails.

blocks.html:
Compliance rules protect the consumer, the company, and your job. Here is every guideline and why it matters:

  1. Say you're on a recorded line with America's Health. Consumers have a right to know who is calling and that the call is recorded.
  2. Double confirm Medicare Parts A and B. Only people with Parts A and B qualify. Double-confirming prevents bad transfers.
  3. Confirm ZIP code and state. Plans vary by area. The specialist needs the right location.
  4. Verify they don't have insurance through an employer or the VA (retirement, military, etc.). Those people aren't a fit.
  5. Tell them they are transferring to a specialist. No surprises. They know who they're about to talk to.
  6. Wait for verbal confirmation to transfer. You MUST ask for the okay and wait for permission before you click transfer. This is the ONLY time you ask for permission on the call.
  7. Stop talking once the agent connects. They usually ask who they're speaking with. Once the lead responds, complete the transfer. Cold transfers only.
  8. May and maybe are your best friends. Always say may or maybe when mentioning something the lead may qualify for.
  9. Stick to the script. Going off script and freestyling is where compliance is broken the most.
  10. NEVER ask the consumer to read or give you a Medicare number or Social Security number. The script only asks whether they know one. The licensed agent handles the actual numbers.

blocks.title: Failing compliance is improper call handling
blocks.html: Not following compliance guidelines is on the zero-tolerance list. Know these cold.

blocks.question: Where is compliance broken the most?
choices: Leaving the conference call
Reading the rebuttals
Confirming the ZIP code
Going off script and freestyling
blocks.explanation: Stay scripted. Freestyling is where compliance breaks most.

blocks.question: Why do you tell the consumer they're being transferred to a specialist?
choices: So the consumer can hang up first
It's optional; you can skip it
It's a compliance rule so the consumer knows who they're about to talk to
Because the specialist is from the government
blocks.explanation: Telling them they're transferring to a specialist is a required compliance step.

blocks.question: The consumer lost their card. What does the script have you ask about their Medicare number or Social Security number?
choices: Ask them to read you their Medicare number
Ask for the last four digits of their Social Security number
Ask whether they KNOW either number, without asking them to give it to you
Skip it and transfer
blocks.explanation: You only ask whether they know one of the numbers. Never ask them to read or give it to you; the licensed agent handles the actual numbers.

blocks.html: You don't know what any consumer will qualify for. Nobody does until the specialist reviews it. So any time you talk about something they could get, you say may or maybe.

• Right: "you may be ENTITLED to some additional food benefits"
  • Wrong: "you ARE entitled to additional food benefits"
  • Wrong: "you're getting a food card"

blocks.title: Never drop the may
blocks.html: The script and rebuttals already have "may" in the right places. If you rush and drop it, you just made a promise. Slow down on those words.

blocks.question: Which statement is compliant?
choices: You qualify for additional benefits
You're definitely getting a food card
You may qualify for additional benefits
Everyone on Medicare gets these benefits
blocks.explanation: Always use may or maybe for anything they could qualify for.

blocks.html:
There is one permission ask on the whole call: "Give them JUST a few minutes to go over them with you, okay?" You MUST wait for a verbal yes before you click transfer. If they say no, read an EXTRA NOT INTERESTED rebuttal and ask again.

You never transfer someone who hasn't said yes. And you don't ask permission anywhere else (like "is it okay if I ask you some questions?"). That just invites a no.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Perfect, well that is EVERYTHING I need. So, a Medicare specialist is coming on the line now to review the additional food benefits for you. Give them JUST a few minutes to go over them with you, okay?

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Alright, so you'll hear a little bit of ringing, that's just me connecting them in, and once they pick up they'll ask you for your name, okay?

blocks.title: Stay scripted
blocks.html: If you forget a line, look at the script. Do not make something up. A made-up line is the fastest way to break compliance.

blocks.question: When must you wait for a verbal yes?
choices: After the ringing line ("they'll ask you for your name okay?")
After every single question
After "Give them JUST a few minutes to go over them with you, okay?"
After the opening greeting
blocks.explanation: The transfer ask is the ONLY permission ask. Once they say yes, you don't need another okay on the ringing line or after the licensed agent connects.

blocks.html:
Never lie or promise anything to get a transfer. Not a little. Not once. These are automatic fails in simulations and on the final exam:

  • Promising money: "you'll get free money if you transfer"
  • Claiming to be Medicare, Social Security, or the government
  • Promising a dollar amount: "you'll get a card worth a lot every month"
  • Promising approval: "you're guaranteed to qualify"
  • Saying their plan will definitely be better
Why so strict? These consumers trust what you say. A lie hurts them, can get the company in serious trouble, and ends your job here. A transfer you got with a lie is not a win.

blocks.title: If you don't know, don't say it
blocks.html: Use "That would be a great question for the agent once I get you there." and keep going.

blocks.question: A consumer says, "I'll only stay on if you promise I get the card." What do you do?
choices: Promise the card so they stay on
Tell them a dollar amount
Tell them the government guarantees it
Don't promise; use the right rebuttal and keep the "may"
blocks.explanation: Promising benefits is an automatic fail. Nothing is guaranteed.

blocks.question: Which of these is an automatic fail?
choices: Saying "you may be ENTITLED to some additional food benefits"
Reading the DNC disclaimer
Saying "I'm calling from Medicare"
Confirming the consumer's ZIP code
blocks.explanation: Claiming to be Medicare or the government is a lie and an automatic fail.

questions.question: What must you say in the opening for compliance?
choices: That you're calling from Medicare
That you're with America's Health on a recorded line
That the consumer has been approved
That the call is not recorded
questions.explanation: Say you're on a recorded line with America's Health.

questions.question: How many times do you ask for permission on the call?
choices: Twice: at the opening and the transfer
Once, at the transfer ask
Before every question
Never
questions.explanation: The transfer ask is the ONLY permission ask.

questions.question: Which words are "your best friends" for compliance?
choices: May and maybe
Always and never
Guaranteed and definitely
Free and money
questions.explanation: Always say may or maybe for anything they may qualify for.

questions.question: What should you do once the agent connects on the transfer?
choices: Introduce the lead
Keep fluffing about the weather
Tell the agent the lead's ZIP code
Stop talking and let the agent and lead speak
questions.explanation: Stop talking once the agent connects. Cold transfers only.

questions.question: Which statement is an automatic fail?
choices: "You'll get free money if you transfer."
"That would be a great question for the agent once I get you there."
"You may qualify for additional benefits."
"I'm with America's Health."
questions.explanation: Promising money to get a transfer is a lie and an automatic fail.

questions.question: Why confirm the consumer's state and ZIP code?
choices: Plans and benefits vary by area, and it's a compliance step
To mail them a card
To check their credit
It's optional
questions.explanation: Confirming state and ZIP is required.

questions.question: A consumer asks, "Is this the government?" What is true?
choices: You can say you work with Social Security
You must never claim to be the government; you're with America's Health
You should hang up
You can say yes if it helps

questions.question: You forget the next line. What do you do?
choices: Skip to the transfer
Ask the consumer what they want to talk about
Make up something close
Look at the script and read it
questions.explanation: Stay scripted. Freestyling is where compliance breaks most.

questions.question: Can you tell a consumer "You're guaranteed approval"?
choices: No, never promise approval
Only on a callback
Yes, if they have Medicaid
Yes, if they qualified on every question
questions.explanation: Promising guaranteed approval is an automatic fail.

questions.question: What does the insurance through work or VA check protect against?
choices: Wrong numbers
Robo calls
Consumers who are busy
Transferring people with employer, retirement or military coverage who aren't a fit
questions.explanation: Verify no employer or VA insurance (retirement, military, etc.).

questions.question: A consumer worries they'll have to give you their Medicare number or Social Security number. What is true?
choices: You should code them Not Interested
You never ask them to read or give either one; you only ask whether they know one, and the licensed agent handles the number
You should read the DNC disclaimer
You should skip the rest of the questions and transfer
questions.explanation: Never ask a consumer to read or give their Medicare or Social Security number. The script only asks whether they know one.
